lines.text: Numbers tell stories. Today you collect real data, let AI help you read it, and check that the story is true.
Ask one clear question with a few choices, like what is your favourite sport.
Keep it anonymous, so nobody writes their name.
Make sure every person can pick exactly one answer.
Put the answers in a spreadsheet, one answer per row.
Use a formula like COUNTIF to count each choice for you.
The sheet does the maths, and you can check it.
Paste only the counts into the AI, never names or personal details.
Ask for the percentages, three findings, and its working.
A summary is only useful if the numbers are right.
AI often slips with maths, so check the total and each percentage yourself.
Percentages for one question should add up to about one hundred.
If a number is wrong, fix it before it goes in your report.
Use a bar chart to compare choices and a pie chart to show parts of one whole.
Use a line chart for change over time, like rainfall each month.
Always give the chart a title and labels.
Each student gets a code like S zero one instead of a name, so the survey stays anonymous.
COUNTIF counts how many times each sport appears, and SUM checks the total.
Twenty five answers in, twenty five counted, so the counting is correct.
The AI showed its working, which makes it easy for us to check.
Three divided by twenty five is twelve percent, not fifteen, so the total comes to one hundred and three.
Finding one says more than half chose cricket, but forty eight percent is less than half.
Two mistakes caught, just by checking the maths ourselves.
You make the chart in the spreadsheet yourself, straight from the checked counts.
A clear title and labels tell the reader exactly what the chart shows.
Your report has the question, a chart, three findings, and an honest label.
If the AI helped, say so, and say that you checked the numbers.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
